binding-1.title: Role-block cards: split the card vector into fixed role sub-spaces with one pooling score per role
binding-1.target: reasoner / store-retrieval blocking weakness: one pooled vector serves both key and value (premonition/model.py:171-197), pool mass 0.979 on the value token, person decodable 116/2048; two-pool and mean-pool both already failed (m03)
binding-1.mechanism: Today one softmax score per token produces one pooled vector; whichever field wins the softmax race erases the other. Two-pool split key from value but each is still one vector built by one competing softmax, so the same race just happens twice. Instead give the pooling head R=4 scores per token (a single Linear(d,R), ~512 extra params) and let each score pool the line into its OWN slice of the card: slice 1 = who, slice 2 = what relation, slice 3 = the value, slice 4 = free. The card is still one 128-d row and one dot product, but 'who' and 'what it says' now live in disjoint coordinates and physically cannot overwrite each other. The retrieval key is read from the who+relation slices only,...
binding-1.gain: Supplied-card choosing is 166-182/512 (32-36%), below a 53.7% question-blind shortcut. If the loss really is the pooled collapse, a role-block card should put choosing clearly above 53.7% and raise pooled->person probe accuracy from ~130/2048 toward the reader-state level (2304/2304). Cost is under 1k parameters.
binding-1.test: On the existing toy ladder (scripts/premonition_ovn_ladder.py) run three arms with identical data and 3 seeds each: (a) baseline D-card-bypass+qread, (b) D-two-pool (already coded, as the fair 'more pools' control), (c) role-block writer. Score exp1 choose:one_hop on validation plus the existing pooled->person / pooled->value linear probes. Role-block wins only if BOTH choosing goes up and both probes stay high; if only the probes improve, the card format (not the pool) is the limiter. Minutes per arm on the 5070 Ti.
binding-1.risks: Two pooling variants have already failed, so the prior on 'more pooling capacity' should be low: the real bottleneck may be that the decoder is never TOLD which field is which (see binding-4). Fixed role assignment may not align with the village's line grammar, and with R=4 each slice is only 32 dims, which may be too thin at d=128. Slice usage can still collapse (three dead slices) unless you mon...

binding-2.title: Multiplicative (HRR/FHRR) binding inside the card: store role-filler pairs in one vector and unbind to read them
binding-2.target: store-retrieval blocking weakness: one pooled card cannot hold person + relation + value; binder writes the SAME value into every entity slot (premonition/model.py:471-481), so roles are indistinguishable
binding-2.mechanism: Vector-symbolic architectures solve exactly this problem with a multiplication-like operator: bind(role, filler) produces a vector that looks like noise, several bound pairs can be ADDED into one vector, and correlating with a role vector pulls its filler back out approximately. Build the card as value = bind(r_who, h_person) + bind(r_rel, h_relation) + bind(r_val, h_value), where the three h vectors are reader states selected by three pooling scores (as in binding-1) and the three role vectors are learned. To ask 'whose card is this', the decoder or the binder unbinds with r_who and compares against the entity slot. Binding is circular convolution (an FFT, cheap and pure PyTorch at d=128) o...
binding-2.gain: A principled ceiling on 'both fields in one vector'. Plausible target: pooled->person and pooled->value probes both near-perfect from the SAME card, choosing above the 53.7% shortcut, and the irrelevant-change flip rate (150/256) falling because the decoder reads a named field rather than whatever dominates the vector.
binding-2.test: Before training anything, run a pure numerical capacity check on the Mac (seconds): at d=128 with 3 roles and realistic vector statistics, how accurately does unbinding recover each filler, and how many superposed pairs before recovery breaks? If 3-role recovery is already noisy at d=128, stop - the idea is dead for this model size. If it survives, train one HRR-card arm against the D-card-bypass baseline on the toy ladder, same data and 2 seeds, and report exp1 choose:one_hop plus the field probes.
binding-2.risks: HRR capacity scales with dimension; d=128 is small for superposing three fillers and unbinding noise may swamp the signal - this is the main reason it could fail here where it works at d=1024+. Circular convolution needs careful initialisation (unit-magnitude Fourier coefficients) or gradients blow up. The Attention-as-Binding paper is a position paper, so its recommendations are untested at any s...

This is that mention turned into a concrete, capacity-checked experiment, and it is the natural successor if binding-1's disjoint slices prov...

binding-3.title: Explicit binding IDs: stamp a per-visit random entity tag onto every card and slot so identity survives any pooling
binding-3.target: evidence blocking weakness: identity is erased at pooling (pooled->person 131/2304) and the binder cannot tell whose card it holds; also reasoner major weakness that long-range identity must pass through a sign-constrained positive minGRU accumulator with one W=64 attention layer
binding-3.mechanism: Mechanistic-interpretability work finds that transformers solve this task by inventing 'binding ID' vectors - an arbitrary tag attached to an entity and copied onto every attribute of that entity, so 'whose is this' is a subspace comparison rather than a content match. D already randomises ENT ids per visit; give each ENT id a tag vector (derived from the tied ENT embedding through a small fixed projection) and ADD that tag into the card value at write time for every entity the line mentions, and into the corresponding entity slot. Nothing has to be learned about where identity lives: after pooling, 'is this Kelo's card' is a dot product with Kelo's tag, by construction. Then the ASK query a...
binding-3.gain: Cheapest of the binding fixes and the most likely to move choosing on its own: identity becomes decodable from the card by construction, so the decoder can reject distractor cards belonging to other people. Watch for choosing rising above 53.7% and for the irrelevant-change flip count (150/256) dropping.
binding-3.test: Toy-ladder A/B with identical data and 3 seeds: D-card-bypass+qread with and without the entity tag added at write time (tag scale is one learned scalar, initialised small so step 0 is bit-identical to the baseline). Primary: exp1 choose:one_hop and the paired irrelevant-change 'both correct and unchanged' count. Secondary: pooled->person probe. Minutes per arm on the 5070 Ti; also run the 2-hop cells since the same tag lets the second query name a person.
binding-3.risks: Adding a fixed tag to every card eats part of the 128-d card budget and may hurt the value read (the mean-pool arm hurt reading 512->363 for a similar reason) - keep the tag scale learned and initialised near zero. A line mentioning several entities gets several tags summed, which is exactly the case the current binder already handles badly. And it only helps if the failure is 'identity absent' ra...

binding-4.title: Give the decoder a typed card row: key + source tag + entity ids + line index, and test the row format independently of the pool
binding-4.target: reasoner blocking weakness: a fetched card enters Think as value + age + row_type only (model.py:458-459), while key, tags, ents, line_start/line_len are written and never read (store.py:43-46); directly answers the project's own OPEN question 'is it the row format or the pooling?'
binding-4.mechanism: Every diagnostic so far has changed the POOL and left the row format alone, so 'pooling is the bottleneck' has never been tested against its obvious alternative. The store already records, for each card, its 64-d retrieval key, a source tag, the entity ids on that line and the line's token span - none of it reaches the model. Concatenate (or add through small projections) the key, a source-tag embedding and a sum of the ENT embeddings for the card's entities into the card's think row. That is a few thousand parameters and no new pooling. If choosing jumps, the row format was the limiter and the whole pooling programme was aimed at the wrong module; if nothing moves, pooling is confirmed and ...
binding-4.gain: A decisive, near-free disambiguation of the project's single biggest open question, plus a plausible direct win on choosing (166-182/512). Even a null result is worth the run: it would make the pool controls the right next spend rather than a guess.
binding-4.test: Exactly the probe the README already names but nobody has run: on the toy ladder, one arm = baseline, one arm = baseline + key and tag and ENT-sum appended to the card row, everything else bit-identical, 3 seeds, score exp1 choose:one_hop. Roughly minutes per arm on the 5070 Ti. Report alongside the pool arms so the two hypotheses are compared on the same axes.
binding-4.risks: The stored key is itself a projection of the collapsed pool, so if the collapse is total the key carries nothing new - this is why the ENT-id sum (which does not pass through the pool) must be in the same row. Adding four signals at once means a positive result does not say which one mattered, so keep a follow-up ablation in reserve. A wider row slightly changes the FLOP accounting.

binding-5.title: Causal swap test: is person identity absent from the card, or present and ignored?
binding-5.target: evidence strength: the project's probe suite is already careful and reproducible across six checkpoints (pooled->person 131/2304, 0.979 pool mass) - but linear probes cannot distinguish 'not there' from 'there but unused', which the vision-prior-art section flags as an unresolved OPEN question
binding-5.mechanism: Probes tell you what a linear reader can extract; they do not tell you what the model uses. The interpretability literature settles exactly this with activation patching: fit the person direction (or the low-dimensional person subspace) on card vectors, then at evaluation time take two cards from the same visit and SWAP only their person components, leaving everything else untouched. If the answer follows the swapped identity, identity is present and the decoder does use it - the failure is an objective problem, and the fix is supervision (binding-6), not representation. If the answer is unmoved, identity is genuinely gone and the writer must change (binding-1/2/3). Do the same swap on the r...
binding-5.gain: Turns the project's most-cited number (pooled->person 116-131/2048) from suggestive into decisive, and routes the next few GPU-days to either the representation fixes or the objective fixes instead of both. Costs no training at all.
binding-5.test: Reuse the six existing probe checkpoints. (1) Fit a linear map from card vectors to person id on held-out visits, take its top few singular directions as the 'person subspace'. (2) On paired evaluation visits, project card A's person component out and add card B's, run the frozen model inside read_only, and count how often the answer follows B. Report against two controls: swapping a random orthogonal direction of the same norm (should do nothing) and swapping the whole card (should flip). Under an hour of Mac CPU.
binding-5.risks: If the person subspace is not linear, a null result is ambiguous - report the random-direction and whole-card controls so the test has a positive and a negative anchor. Patching changes the vector norm unless you renormalise, which can itself perturb the decoder. Small n: use enough paired visits for a visit-clustered interval, not a raw Wilson one.
binding-5.overlap: The project has extensive linear probing and paired counterfactual VISIT edits, but no activation-level patching anywhere. It is the missing causal half of the evidence it already collects, and directly answers final-sweep README's 'representation problem or objective problem?'.

binding-6.title: Supervise choosing directly: a listwise card-selection loss with structured hard negatives on the supplied-card toy
binding-6.target: training major weakness: the exp1 ladder that produced the 166-182/512 'choosing' number trains ONLY answer cross-entropy (scripts/premonition_ovn_ladder.py:316-337), so 'choosing is weak' is partly a statement about a signal that was deliberately removed; also the 150/256 irrelevant-change flips
binding-6.mechanism: There is currently no gradient anywhere that says 'this supplied row is the right one'. Add a small selection head that scores each supplied card row against the question and train it with a listwise cross-entropy whose negatives are deliberately structured: same person / different relation, same relation / different person, same value / different owner. Those are the three confusions the failure analysis actually shows. Pair it with an invariance term: the answer distribution must not move when an irrelevant card is edited, and must move when the relevant one is. If choosing goes from 32-36% to well above the 53.7% shortcut with no architectural change, then three pooling experiments were chasing an absent-supervision problem; if it does not move, the representation verdict is finally earned.
binding-6.test: On the identical exp1 toy, two arms x 3 seeds: (a) answer CE only (current), (b) answer CE + listwise selection CE over the supplied rows with oracle hard negatives. wording-generalization-1.title: Make question wording its own split axis, and run the matched-facts wording control
wording-generalization-1.target: data-eval blocking weakness: "Question wording is not a separable axis" (learnlab/splits.py:30 AXES has only name/template/teacher_style/rule_family; gate criteria heldout_visible / unseen_templates / unseen_styles all report the identical n=3763, hits=881) and the confounded name_gap (seen 69 vs fresh 229, note admits templates and styles also differ)
wording-generalization-1.mechanism: Right now every held-out question is simultaneously new wording, new teacher style and new names, so the 23.4% number cannot say which one hurts. Split the single "template" axis into three: q_wording (the q.* banks), narration_template, and teacher_style, and add q_wording to the hash manifest so it can be held in or out independently. Then regenerate two extra held-out sets from the same worlds: (A) new world, new names, but TRAIN question phrasings; (B) new world, train names, new phrasings. Score the same saved 4M checkpoint on both. The difference between A and B is the wording penalty with everything else matched. This is the control the pretraining-diversity literature says you need: ...
wording-generalization-1.gain: No accuracy gain by itself — it buys a correct diagnosis. Expected outcome: a number like "held-out accuracy is X% with train phrasings and 23% with new phrasings", which decides whether the next month goes into phrasing data or into architecture. It also removes the ~1.7-point mix artefact already measured in the generalisation_gap if you reweight per-type at the same time.
wording-generalization-1.test: Add q_wording to AXES in learnlab/splits.py, regenerate 600 validation visits twice (74 s per 20k visits, so this is seconds), and re-score the existing 4M checkpoint from run 20260919T092801Z on both sets (final eval takes 5.5 s). Control: the existing held-out set scored by the same checkpoint in the same call. Report Wilson intervals but note clustering. Total: under 30 minutes of work, no training.
wording-generalization-1.risks: The split machinery has canaries and a SplitLeak audit, so adding an axis may require re-deriving the manifest and will invalidate comparability with earlier runs; you must keep the old axes bit-identical for the old sets. If A and B come out similar, the wording story is wrong and the collapse is about names or styles — that is still a useful answer but will feel like a wasted day.

latent-thought-5.mechanism: Premonition has something most latent-reasoning papers do not: an oracle that knows the exact chain of evidence lines. tiny-lm-training-1.title: Add a cooldown (WSD) to every run and keep the best-on-validation checkpoint, then re-test the seed split
tiny-lm-training-1.target: training weakness: 'There is no learning-rate decay anywhere - warmup then a constant LR' (learnlab/train.py:100-102 lr_at, confirmed by reading the file); and the blocking 'Seed instability is measured but not managed' (503/512 seed 0 vs 27/512 seed 1 at 1,405 matched steps)
tiny-lm-training-1.mechanism: Today both trainers warm the learning rate up and then hold it flat until the last step, so the model is still taking big noisy steps when you stop and score it. The standard modern fix is Warmup-Stable-Decay: keep the flat phase, but spend the last 10-20% of the budget decaying the learning rate to (near) zero. Most of the final loss drop happens in that cooldown, and the decay is what turns a noisy high-variance endpoint into a settled one. memory-store-7.mechanism: A memory layer replaces one feed-forward block with a very large trainable key-value table that each token reads only a few entries from (product keys split the lookup into two halves so search stays cheap). Parameters rise hugely; FLOPs barely move. The continual-learning payoff is the part the vision wants: because each fact lives in a handful of slots, you can finetune ONLY the slots a new fact activates relative to background usage, and old skills survive. Meta's follow-up measured this precisely. That is the mechanism 'weights change only in sleep' needs, and it drops into the Core 4M transformer with no reasoner redesign.

eval-methodology-4.title: Power-first eval-set construction: generate to a target n per cell instead of generating visits and hoping
eval-methodology-4.target: data-eval STRENGTH: generation is nearly free (20,000 train visits in 74.2 s; 600 validation visits in ~6.3 s; whole final eval in 5.46 s). Weaknesses it repairs: 7 of 17 leak classes fall below the 100-item floor and can never return clean (contents n=9); the counterfactual-twin test is n=210 with p=0.048 against alpha=0.01
eval-methodology-4.mechanism: The project treats eval-set size as whatever falls out of generating N visits, and then discovers afterwards that a cell has 9 items and cannot be tested. Invert it. Decide first, per cell, the smallest effect you care about (e.g. leak detector 5 points above its null, per the existing LEAK_MARGIN; counterfactual twins beating a 6.4% chance rate), compute the n that gives you 80% power at alpha=0.01 including the design effect from idea 2, and then generate until each cell reaches that n - rejection-sampling visits by question type if the scheduler will not produce rare types densely enough. For the twin test, the binding number is the LINK YIELD (1,200 pair-visits produced only 210 usable t...
eval-methodology-4.gain: Every leak class becomes testable (removing the current situation where the panel is silent on exactly the classes slices.py already flags as suspect), and the counterfactual-twin criterion becomes a real pass/fail instead of a coin flip. Cost is minutes of generation against decisions worth GPU-days.
eval-methodology-4.test: Pure arithmetic first, no code: for the twin test at chance 6.37%, compute the n needed to detect the observed 9.52% at alpha=0.01 with 80% power (a one-proportion power calculation), and the pair-visit count that implies at the current 210/1200 link yield. Do the same for the 'contents' class against its 100-item floor. If the required generation is under an hour, the decision makes itself; the matched control is simply re-scoring the SAME checkpoint on the enlarged set and checking the point estimate does not move while the interval shrinks.

eval-methodology-5.title: Replace linear probes with interchange interventions before committing to the pooling diagnosis
eval-methodology-5.target: evidence strength that is actually load-bearing: "ESTABLISHED (mechanism). The information loss happens at pooling" rests on linear decodability (pooled->person 131/2304, 97.9% attention mass on the value token). The final-sweep README itself calls the probe story 'plausible-not-settled', and three pooling repairs have now failed
eval-methodology-5.mechanism: A linear probe answers 'is this information present in a readable form', which is necessary but not sufficient for 'the model uses this information'. The causal test is an interchange intervention: take two visits, run both, then copy the card vector (or a subspace of it) from visit B into visit A at the point where the decoder reads it, and check whether A's answer becomes what the high-level story says it should become. The fraction of such swaps where the model's output matches the predicted output is interchange intervention accuracy (IIA). eval-methodology-5.gain: Either confirms the pooling diagnosis with causal rather than correlational evidence (so the pool-control arm is worth running), or shows the person information IS used and the failure is downstream in choosing - which would redirect the whole sweep. Given that three pooling repairs have already failed, the second outcome is live and would save a lot of wasted arms.
eval-methodology-5.test: On an existing checkpoint, no training: for 256 matched visit pairs, run the model normally, then re-run visit A with the card store's value vector for one card replaced by the corresponding card from visit B (three conditions: whole vector, key only, value only). Score how often A's answer becomes B's answer. Matched control: swap a card that is irrelevant to A's question - that should change nothing. The existing counterfactual-pair harness already builds the pairs.

eval-methodology-6.title: Score toy runs with a continuous progress measure so that 0/512-vs-503/512 stops being the unit of evidence
eval-methodology-6.target: evidence/training weaknesses: results are reported as exact-match counts that jump between chance and near-perfect (27/512 vs 503/512; choose 166-182/512); no best-on-validation checkpointing exists (train_d saves only the final model), so a run that learns then collapses is unrecoverable
eval-methodology-6.mechanism: Exact-match accuracy is a discontinuous metric: it can sit at chance for a long time while the underlying representation improves steadily, then jump. That is the documented mechanism behind apparent 'emergence' - swap to a continuous metric and the jump often disappears. For Premonition the natural continuous measures already exist as logged quantities: log-probability margin of the gold answer over the best distractor value, gold recall@4 minus the random-fetch baseline, pool attention entropy, and probe accuracy on person vs value. Log these at every eval_every, and (a) use them to keep the best-on-validation checkpoint instead of the last one, and (b) use them as the screening metric whe...
eval-methodology-6.gain: Lets you rank arms with far fewer steps per arm (screen on the smooth measure, confirm on exact match), recovers runs that peaked mid-training, and distinguishes 'this seed failed' from 'this seed was not finished'. Given every Premonition arm currently costs 1,405-3,750 steps to produce one discrete number, this could multiply arms-per-GPU-hour several times over.
eval-methodology-6.test: Re-score existing checkpoints (or re-run one arm with extra logging) to emit the gold-answer log-odds margin at each eval point alongside the exact-match count. Then check the key claim empirically: does the margin at step 400 rank the five seeds in the same order as exact-match at step 1,405? Spearman correlation on 5 points is weak but decisive enough to justify or reject the screening use. Minutes on the GPU.

eval-methodology-7.mechanism: The project's entire decision procedure is 'screen arms cheaply on the toy ladder, then build the winner'. That procedure is only valid if the cheap setting ranks arms the same way the expensive setting does, and nobody has checked. The check is a small designed experiment: take the 5-6 arms already scored in SUMMARY.txt, re-run all of them in the expensive setting (5070 Ti, step-matched rather than FLOP-matched, 3-5x the steps, multiple seeds per idea 1) and compute the rank correlation between cheap-setting ranking and expensive-setting ranking. eval-methodology-7.gain: Either a licence to keep screening cheaply (huge, since it makes the rest of the plan sound) or early discovery that the screen is invalid (also huge, and much cheaper to learn now than after three more conditional arms). Also removes the step-count confound from every development A/B.
eval-methodology-7.test: Pick the 5 arms in SUMMARY.txt that already have test numbers, re-run each step-matched at 2 seeds on the 5070 Ti at ~4x the original step count, and compute Spearman rank correlation between the cheap ranking and the expensive ranking. With 5 arms the correlation is noisy, so precommit the decision rule: if the top-2 arms in the cheap setting are not the top-2 in the expensive setting, stop trusting the cheap screen. A handful of GPU-hours at most.
eval-methodology-7.risks: Five arms gives very low statistical resolution on a rank correlation - this is a smoke test, not a proof, and should be described that way. eval-methodology-8.title: A test-set budget with a precommitted decision log, because the pilot already consulted the test set
eval-methodology-8.target: training/data-eval STRENGTH: "Strong experiment hygiene in the overnight scripts: validation used for development, test scored once behind a guard" (scripts/premonition_ovn_ladder.py:582-595), plus digest-pinned identity and read_only evaluation. Weakness it repairs: evidence OPEN item - "Held-out numbers combine validation and test, and test was consulted during the iterative pilot"
eval-methodology-8.mechanism: The guard machinery is already good; what is missing is accounting. Every time a test number is looked at and influences the next decision, a little of the test set's independence is spent - this is adaptive overfitting, and the standard remedies are to budget the number of adaptive looks, to answer test queries through a noise-adding or thresholding mechanism (the Ladder: only report a new test score when it beats the previous best by more than a threshold), and above all to log every look. Concretely: add a test-query ledger file that records, for each test evaluation, the date, the checkpoint digest, the arm, and the decision it fed; make cmd_test append to it automatically; and precommit...
eval-methodology-8.gain: Restores the ability to make an official verdict. The project's own identity.guard_verdict already returns full_verdict:false and the evidence audit flags that test was consulted during the pilot; a ledger plus fresh test identities makes a clean primary result possible again, which is a precondition for any 'D beats A' claim.
eval-methodology-8.test: Two parts, both cheap. (1) Grep the artifacts and reviews for every recorded test evaluation and write the historical ledger retrospectively - this alone tells you how many adaptive looks have been spent. (2) Generate one fresh test split with a new seed (~6 s), re-score the current best checkpoint on both the old and the fresh test split, and compare. If the two agree within the clustered interval from idea 2, the old test set is not yet badly spent; if the fresh split is meaningfully worse, adaptive overfitting is real and measured.
eval-methodology-8.risks: Fresh test splits are only interchangeable if the generator is fixed - any pattern-bank top-up or scheduler change makes old and new test sets non-comparable, so the fresh-split trick must be pinned to the same digest-verified generator version. Also a single fresh-split comparison is itself noisy; treat a small gap as uninformative rather than as a clean bill of health.

sequence-backbones-1.mechanism: A Canon layer is almost the cheapest thing you can add to a sequence model: h'_t = h_t + conv1d over [h_t, h_{t-1}, h_{t-2}, h_{t-3}] with learnable per-channel weights (a causal depthwise convolution of kernel 4, with a residual). sequence-backbones-2.title: Let the recurrent state cancel: replace the positive-only log-space minGRU scan with a real-space scan whose decay can be negative (or a delta-rule update)
sequence-backbones-2.target: Weakness (major): 'The recurrent memory is sign-constrained' — _log_g makes h_t strictly positive, so the reader state can only accumulate and decay, never erase or flip (premonition/model.py:46-70). All long-range within-visit binding passes through this positive accumulator, and a line's card is pooled from these states.
sequence-backbones-2.mechanism: Grazzi et al. proved that a linear RNN whose state-transition eigenvalues live in [0,1] cannot solve parity, and cannot do the 'flip / oscillate' style of state tracking at all, because positive eigenvalues make the state converge or diverge monotonically. neuro-inspired-1.target: Blocking weakness: one pooled vector produces both the card key and the card value, so addressing and reading fight over one softmax (0.979 pool mass on the value token; card person linearly decodable in only 116/2048 probes). premonition/model.py:171-197 (CardWriter), premonition/card_pools.py.
neuro-inspired-1.mechanism: In the hippocampus the thing that identifies a memory is not a compressed copy of the memory. synthetic-data-world-5.title: Stop reusing the corpus 13.7 times: scale the medium preset to roughly one epoch and redo 4M vs 28M at token parity
synthetic-data-world-5.target: data-eval STRENGTH: "World generation and evaluation are both extremely cheap" — 20,000 train visits in 74.2 s, full final eval 5.46 s — currently wasted, because training reuses 24.15M tokens for 13.735 epochs and the 28M-vs-4M comparison is exposure-confounded (119M vs 396M tokens)
synthetic-data-world-5.mechanism: Generation costs about 74 seconds per 20,000 visits, so 200,000 visits costs roughly 12 minutes of wall clock and gives about 240M tokens — enough for the 600 s 4M run to see each visit roughly once. That single change removes two confounds at once: the memorisation component of the 44% train-split vs 23.4% held-out gap (a 4M model at 8-16 epochs with a constant learning rate and no regularisation is a textbook memoriser), and the '28M is no better than 4M' claim, which currently compares a model that saw 396M tokens with one that saw 119M. The generator's cheapness is a real strength of this project and it is simply not being spent.
synthetic-data-world-5.gain: Cleanly separates memorisation from the wording problem, and gives the first honest answer to 'is the 4M model data-limited or capacity-limited?' — which the final-sweep README already admits is unresolved. Also makes every later A/B on the Core track less noisy, because arms stop differing in how many times they saw the corpus.
synthetic-data-world-5.test: Generate 200k train visits (~12 min). Then three 600 s runs on the 5070 Ti: (a) 4M on the current 24M-token corpus (the existing control), (b) 4M on the 240M-token corpus, (c) 28M on the 240M corpus stopped at the SAME token count as (b), not the same seconds. synthetic-data-world-5.risks: Disk: 20k visits is 236 MB, so 200k is roughly 2.4 GB — check space before generating. At token parity the 28M model gets fewer optimiser steps, so a null result still will not fully settle capacity; say so up front. And if one-epoch training simply lowers all the numbers, the project loses its familiar baseline — keep the 24M corpus and its checkpoint around as the reference.

trace-supervision-2.title: Answer-token weighting as the honest control arm, done with a float weight not a boolean mask
trace-supervision-2.target: training/data-eval major weakness: learnlab/core.py:110-122 lm_loss weights every target identically and the loss mask is boolean, so there is nowhere to put a weight; 'upweight answer tokens' has been diagnosed twice with no code change.
trace-supervision-2.mechanism: Before believing that traces help, you have to rule out the boring explanation: traces help only because they put more gradient near the answer. The control is to keep the corpus exactly as it is and instead multiply the per-token loss of answer tokens by a constant (say 3, 10, 30), which is a two-line change from a boolean mask to a float weight. Rho-1 showed that choosing which tokens carry loss, rather than which tokens exist, is itself a large lever: selecting useful tokens matched a much more expensive baseline with 3% of the pretraining tokens. If a plain weight recovers most of the trace arm's gain, the trace is not buying reasoning, only attention.

memory-net-era-autopsy-6.mechanism: Premonition already pays for the expensive half of PonderNet and throws the benefit away. Deep supervision computes a loss L_n at every loop n, then averages them flat (divided by question-loop pairs). That single change does three things at once. It gives later loops a way to matter (if loop 5 is better, p_5 grows and loop 5's loss dominates — the flat average can never express that). memory-net-era-autopsy-7.mechanism: Every mechanism Premonition has for comparing cards is attention: a query dotted against keys, then a weighted read.
